source: Dhami, Belton, Mandel (2019) The analysis of competing hypotheses in intelligence analysis
finding: 50 UK analysts, half trained in ACH (half-day) and told to use it, half not. On a 4-hypothesis, 12-cue task with a known Bayes answer, ACH did not raise the chance of picking the right tribe.
numbers: Correct top hypothesis (Conda): ACH 9/25 (36%), control 8/25 (33%), chi2(1,N=49)=.04, p=.845. Fully correct rank order: ACH 1/25, control 2 of the 16 who could be scored. Tied ranks: ACH 80% vs control 19%, p<.001.
limits: One small, simple, fully specified task; analysts had mean 14 months of experience; groups ran on the same training day.
agent_relevance: Hand-run ACH gave no accuracy gain even when every cue and probability was handed over. A matrix scaffold alone does not buy correct answers.
quote: ACH-trained analysts did not follow all of the steps of ACH.

source: Dhami et al. (2019), step adherence in the ACH group
finding: Even trained and instructed, most analysts broke the ACH scoring rule. Only 5 of 25 used inconsistent evidence only; 19 summed both consistent and inconsistent evidence.
numbers: Inconsistent-only integration: ACH 5/25 (20%), control 0; both types: ACH 19 (76%) vs control 16 of 20 (78%). Applied the evidence scoring rule consistently across items: ACH 1/25 (4%) vs control 4 of 9 who used a rule (44%), p=.003. Final conclusion matched own matrix: ACH 16/25 (64%) vs control all assessable analysts, p=.007.
limits: Control cells are small; scoring needed a written rule.
agent_relevance: The disconfirm-only rule is unnatural. The agent should not expect a model to follow it stably and should not add it as a step.
quote: Authors say these are significant departures from ACH, yet analysts would believe they applied ACH.

source: Dhami et al. (2019), base rates and diagnosticity
finding: ACH raised attention to evidence diagnosticity but cut use of base rates. The control group used base rates far more often.
numbers: Used base rates: ACH 3/25 (12%) vs control 13/25 (52%), chi2=9.19, p=.002. Considered diagnosticity: ACH 20/25 (80%) vs control 8/25 (32%), p=.001. Sensitivity analysis: ACH 15/25 vs control 1/25, p<.001. Identified all 12 cues: ACH 92% vs control 68%, p=.034.
limits: Base rates were given in the task text; real tasks may not have clean priors.
agent_relevance: A matrix of evidence rows crowds out priors. Any hypothesis table in the agent needs an explicit prior column.
quote: ACH does not provide any guidance on the use of base rates.

source: Dhami et al. (2019), matrix use without ACH
finding: The matrix is something untrained analysts build by themselves. 80% of the control group reformatted the data; 16 of 25 drew a matrix.
numbers: Reformatted data: ACH 25/25 vs control 20/25, p=.018. Of 20 control reformatters, 16 drew a matrix (14 with hypotheses as columns), 4 made a list.
limits: Controls came from an organisation that trains ACH, so earlier exposure cannot be ruled out.
agent_relevance: The matrix layer is cheap and natural. The harm, where found, sits in the scoring and integration steps.

source: Mandel, Karvetski, Dhami (2018) Boosting intelligence analysts' judgment accuracy: what works, what fails?
finding: Same 50 analysts (25 per arm). ACH did not improve probability accuracy; the control arm was a little better. Coherence was also a little worse with ACH.
numbers: MAE vs naive Bayes: ACH .26 vs control .21, difference .04 [-.02,.11], d about 0.43-0.45, p=.14 (probability of superiority .62 for control). Sum of the 4 hypothesis probabilities: ACH 1.77 vs control 1.54 (ideal 1.0). Share of error that is quantity disagreement: ACH .73 vs control .50, p=.04.
limits: N=25 per arm, so underpowered for medium effects. Task is a toy with a three-level score.
agent_relevance: ACH made the unitarity error (probabilities summing above 1) larger. Code should normalise any probability the model emits.
quote: Although ACH failed to improve accuracy, we found that recalibration and aggregation methods substantially improved accuracy.

source: Mandel et al. (2018), information usefulness
finding: ACH did improve judging which cues are useful, but that skill did not carry into accuracy.
numbers: Correlation of usefulness ratings with true probability gain: ACH .68 [.61,.75] vs control .17 [-.02,.35], d=1.59, p<.001. Usefulness-tracking correlated with error r=-.42 in control (p=.045) and r=-.10 in ACH (p=.63). Rank correlation of judgments with Bayes: ACH .29 vs control .24, p=.78.
limits: Authors call the control-group correlation unanticipated and in need of replication.
agent_relevance: Diagnosticity rating is learnable and ACH helps it. The failure is in the aggregation step, which suggests letting code do the aggregation.

source: Mandel et al. (2018), recalibration and aggregation
finding: Statistical post-processing helped far more than ACH. Making judgments sum correctly and then averaging across analysts cut error by 61%.
numbers: MAE fell 61% after coherentizing then aggregating. Most of the gain came with small groups (two to three analysts). Analysts beat random responses (MAE .23 vs .33, d=.95).
limits: Aggregating random draws also pulls responses towards .25, so some gain is variance reduction. Needs several judges.
agent_relevance: Supports a code-side step: normalise to sum 1 and average several samples, rather than adding a matrix procedure.

source: Karvetski and Mandel (2020) Coherence of probability judgments from uncertain evidence: Does ACH help?
finding: 227 educated adults judged 6 graffiti cases with uncertain evidence (source reliability and credibility codes). ACH vs no technique: no advantage on any coherence test.
numbers: N=227 (ACH vs control). Binary choice consistent with probability: no method effect (t(218)=1.14, p=.25, d=0.15); overall match .74. Agreement with Bayes on top hypothesis: .65, no method effect. Mean absolute deviation from Bayes .31 raw, .33 normalised, no method effect.
limits: Online sample, not analysts. Evidence given as verbal terms and codes.
agent_relevance: The most realistic-evidence test, and a clean null. It also shows no harm on coherence.
quote: The findings do not support the claim that ACH is effective at improving probabilistic judgment.

source: Karvetski and Mandel (2020), reliability
finding: ACH made judgments slightly less reliable across structurally identical cases.
numbers: Mean absolute deviation between isomorphic case pairs: ACH .22 [.19,.24] vs control .18 [.16,.20]; method F=3.86, p=.05 (.051), d=0.20.
limits: Borderline p; small effect. The idea that costs are largest for the best analysts is untested.
agent_relevance: ACH adds noise. Same case in, different answer out is a direct risk for a scaffold.

source: Karvetski and Mandel (2020), pseudo-diagnosticity
finding: ACH users gave non-neutral consistency ratings to non-diagnostic evidence. Non-diagnostic evidence had about 30-32% of the impact of fully diagnostic evidence.
numbers: Mixed regression of differential consistency on scaled evidence: intercept B=0.233 (SE .074, p=.002), slope B=0.502 (SE .082, p<.001), R2=.055. Non-diagnostic impact about 32% of diagnostic. Alternative coding: intercept .522, slope 1.20, about 30%.
limits: Consistency ratings were not taken from the control group, so a similar bias in controls cannot be excluded.
agent_relevance: Weak evidence must not push a hypothesis score. Weights should come from stated source quality, not from the model's feel.

source: Karvetski and Mandel (2020), conservatism and subadditivity
finding: Both groups under-updated and both gave probabilities that summed above 1 for binary complements. ACH changed neither.
numbers: Conservatism: distance from 50/50 was .13 [.11,.14] for elicited vs .33 [.31,.35] for Bayes, t(226)=23.20, d=1.54. Bias from complementarity: method F=1.52, p=.22; higher evidential support gave more subadditivity (F=5.04, p<.001; r=.29).
limits: Bayes comparison depends on each person's own verbal-term translations.
agent_relevance: Humans (and probably models) under-update. A matrix does not fix that; an explicit likelihood-ratio update might.

source: Karvetski, Mandel, Irwin (2020) Improving probability judgment in intelligence analysis: from structured analysis to statistical aggregation
finding: ACH was pitted against a factorized Bayes method (FBT) with a before/after design. ACH made probability judgments less coherent and less accurate than the same people's earlier no-method judgments.
numbers: N=147 Canadian graduates; mushroom task, 3 hypotheses. ACH x timing on bias from unitarity F(1,141)=22.12, p<.0001; on additivity F(1,141)=4.18, p=.04. Coherentization raised accuracy about 1 SD (average d=1.10).
limits: Online sample; invented task; coherentization gains also appear with random data, so part is mechanical.
agent_relevance: Within-person design removes between-person noise, so this is the cleanest harm result. The helpful part was the post-analytic code step.
quote: ACH was the least effective method, actually reducing accuracy and coherence compared to a within-subject no-method control.

source: Karvetski, Mandel, Irwin (2020), correlated cues
finding: ACH users double counted two perfectly correlated cues, more so when the correlation was made visually salient.
numbers: In the factorized Bayes arm, mean distance between conditional probabilities for the two correlated cues was 0.14 (SD .19) high-salience vs 0.27 (SD .25) low-salience, t(53.7)=2.15, p=.036, d=0.56. In ACH, more row-copying (double counting) under high salience.
limits: Single study, mushroom task.
agent_relevance: A row-per-item matrix counts dependent sources twice. The agent should cluster dependent evidence before scoring.

source: Karvetski, Mandel, Irwin (2020), aggregation
finding: All aggregation forms improved accuracy; most of the gain came by group size about 10; much of it is variance reduction, since random responses also gained.
numbers: Equal weighting was most robust at small group size. Bayes computed from elicited parts, once aggregated, was most accurate for groups over 7. ACH post-method raw aggregates were less accurate than pre-method ones.
limits: Coherence-weighted aggregation helped ACH at larger sizes but was worst for the Bayes arm; no single ranking.
agent_relevance: Ensembling samples and computing posteriors in code from elicited parts beats asking for the final probability.

source: Wilcox and Mandel (2024) Critical review of the Analysis of Competing Hypotheses technique
finding: A search (244 hits) found seven articles on six randomised ACH-vs-no-SAT experiments. ACH has little to no overall benefit on judgment quality and may harm it. No study showed an overall gain.
numbers: Table 3 tally: accuracy non-different (Mandel 2018, Karvetski 2020, Karvetski and Mandel 2020); reliability worse (1 study); base-rate use worse (1); pseudo-diagnosticity and double counting worse (2); confirmation-bias reduction positive only in Lehner 2008 (non-analysts); non-different in Lehner (analysts), Whitesmith, Maegherman.
limits: No pooled effect size (tasks differ); Google Scholar search only; several experiments with N under 50.
agent_relevance: Best single summary of the null. Supports section 4b: do not add ACH as a mandatory stage.
quote: We consequently discourage intelligence organizations from mandating the training or use of ACH.

source: Wilcox and Mandel (2024), where ACH might go wrong
finding: The review names four causes: ignoring confirming evidence; vague 'consistency'; cognitive burden and misdirected attention; wrong audience. It lists what may be useful: the matrix and exhaustive listing.
numbers: 20 of 25 ACH analysts used confirming evidence despite instruction. Matrix helpfulness mean 57.1 (SD 18.8) out of 100 in the law-student study, 62% did not use it. None of the observed ACH benefits had been replicated.
limits: Mechanisms are hypotheses, not tested one by one. Authors do not recommend avoiding ACH, only mandates.
agent_relevance: Gives a clean decomposition to test in an LLM: matrix on, scoring rule off.

source: Lehner, Adelman, Cheikes, Brown (2008) Confirmation bias in complex analyses (via Wilcox and Mandel 2024 and a search abstract)
finding: Only the abstract and the review table were read. ACH reduced confirmation bias for people with no analytic experience, not for experienced analysts, who showed less bias to begin with.
numbers: N=24 in a 2x2 (ACH vs none by experience); 5 experienced analysts in the ACH cell and 7 in the non-SAT cell, per review.
limits: Original MITRE report returned HTTP 403; full text not read.
agent_relevance: The one positive result for ACH is small-sample and novice-only. Do not lean on it.
quote: The study was too underpowered to produce reliable assessments of effects (or non-effects).

source: Whitesmith (2020) as described in Wilcox and Mandel (2024)
finding: 39 King's College London staff and students (32 students, 7 intelligence community staff); ACH gave no significant reduction in confirmation bias or serial-position effects.
numbers: 8 of 39 (21%) showed confirmation bias. Two hours of ACH training.
limits: Participants were told belief need not match ACH final scores, so the scoring rule may not have been followed. Second-hand from the review table.
agent_relevance: Another null on the one effect ACH is meant to fix.

source: Maegherman, Ask, Horselenberg, Koppen (2021) Test of the analysis of competing hypotheses in legal decision-making
finding: 191 law students got either a short ACH explanation or general bias information. Both arms favoured exonerating questions; ACH did not change guilt judgments or search for information.
numbers: N=191. Only 38% of ACH participants complied and reported using the matrix (per review).
limits: Abstract (Semantic Scholar record) and review table only; the task showed no baseline bias, so no room for benefit.
agent_relevance: When there is no bias to remove, ACH has nothing to fix. Measure the agent's baseline bias before adding a correction.
quote: Despite the lack of bias observed, it seems participants failed to properly apply the ACH method.

source: Dhami et al. (2024) Effects of task structure and confirmation bias in alternative hypotheses evaluation, Study 1
finding: N=161 students saw the same task in three layouts. Only hypotheses-in-rows reduced reliance on confirming evidence; the ACH matrix (hypotheses in columns) did not.
numbers: Chi2(2)=9.43, p=.009, phi=.24. Overall 56.5% picked the confirmation-only answer. Hypotheses in rows: Bonferroni p=.003 for fewer confirm-only choices. ACH-style matrix: p=.327; paragraph: p=.048 (borderline). Credibility sensitivity: 77% (ACH matrix), 78% (rows), 75% (text), chi2(2)=.15, p=.927.
limits: Students, 90% female, mean age 20; authors call for replication; only two hypotheses, 12 items.
agent_relevance: Layout alone can shift strategy. For a model, orientation and order of a hypothesis table is a prompt variable to test.
quote: The findings of Study 1 do not support the belief that an ACH-style matrix would improve analytic judgment by eliminating confirmation bias.

source: Dhami et al. (2024), Study 2 and individual differences
finding: 62 Dutch military analysts mostly did not show confirmation bias; most integrated both evidence types and were sensitive to credibility.
numbers: Strategy: 19.4% confirm-only, 14.5% inconsistent-only, 66.1% balanced. 83.3% switched hypothesis when credibility fell. Credibility sensitivity by strategy: balanced 98%, confirm-only 72.7%, inconsistent-only 33.3%. Mean CRT 2.32 (SD .92); CRT unrelated to additivity (r=-.12, p=.374). In Study 1 low CRT predicted confirm-only (Glass d=0.54).
limits: Small N; strategy classified from 2-3 tasks.
agent_relevance: Disconfirm-only users were worst on credibility (33%). Pure refutation is not a safe rule.

source: Martin (2025) Relationship between structured analytic techniques and intelligence analysis quality: content analysis
finding: Content analysis of 138 reports from two experimental analysis challenges. ACH was rarely used and its accuracy correlation was slightly negative.
numbers: n=138 reports. Correlation with accuracy: ACH r=-0.08, timeline r=.28, Bayes theorem r=.22, evidence table r=.19. Of the 12 primer SATs only ACH and Key Assumptions Check were used more than once. ACH code reliability 0.79 [0.32,1.00].
limits: Correlational, not randomised; teams chose techniques; low power.
agent_relevance: In natural use, Bayes and timeline work correlated a little better with accuracy than ACH. Still weak.

source: Heuer (1999) Psychology of Intelligence Analysis, chapter 8 (CIA edition)
finding: The founding claim: ACH is 'a surprisingly effective, proven process', an eight-step matrix procedure. The chapter gives argument and a 1998 India nuclear test example, no experiment.
numbers: No numbers. Steps: hypotheses, evidence list, matrix with diagnosticity, refine, try to disprove, sensitivity, report, milestones. Says holding three to seven hypotheses in working memory is beyond most people.
limits: The claim of proof is not backed by controlled data in the text read.
agent_relevance: The working-memory argument is the main rationale. A model with a long context lacks that limit, which weakens the case for the matrix.
quote: It is a surprisingly effective, proven process that helps analysts avoid common analytic pitfalls.

source: Chang, Berdini, Mandel, Tetlock (2018) Restructuring structured analytic techniques in intelligence (not opened; cited in papers read)
finding: Cited by Karvetski and Mandel and by Wilcox and Mandel for two problems with SATs: bipolar biases (fixing one can cause its opposite) and noise neglect (many vague steps add error).
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Second-hand from papers read.
agent_relevance: Frames the main risk of adding a stage: more steps, more variance.

source: Coulthart (2017) review of SAT evidence (as cited by Martin 2025)
finding: Of 12 SATs in the US primer, only six had any empirical test, ACH among them. The share of studies supporting each ranged 0 to 100%. Only three had evidence credibility above low.
numbers: No other numbers read. The SUBFIELDS.md row says ACH had moderate to strong support in Coulthart's review; that was not verified here.
limits: Second-hand through Martin 2025; the dissertation and article were not opened. Tone differs from Wilcox and Mandel (2024).
agent_relevance: Conflict to settle in synthesis: Coulthart vs Wilcox and Mandel.

source: Zhao et al. (2025) AgentCDM: ACH-inspired structured reasoning for LLM multi-agent decisions
finding: ACH used as a prompt protocol for a decider agent that reads several agents' answers. Zero-shot it beat an unstructured decider by 1.9 points on average; the trained version gained far more.
numbers: MMLU, MMLU-Pro, ARC-Challenge with glm-4-9b, Llama-3-8B, Mistral-7B, Qwen-2-72B, GPT-4. All-average gain over single agent: unstructured decider -0.7, zero-shot ACH decider +2.3 (table text garbled), trained AgentCDM +7.0 to +7.8. MMLU-Pro: Llama-3-8B +22.5 points, Mistral-7B +29.3 after training.
limits: Gains come mostly from fine-tuning; weak baseline decider; no ablation of matrix vs other parts; multiple-choice benchmarks, not intelligence tasks; no independent replication.
agent_relevance: Zero-shot gain from an ACH-style prompt is small (about 2 points). Not clean proof that the matrix itself helps.
quote: Homogeneous variant surpassing it by 1.9 percentage points on the All Average metric.

source: Zhao et al. (2025) AgentCDM ablation
finding: Training on the rigid scaffold only did worse than a plain prompt. Rigid adherence to the protocol hurt generalisation. Weak models got worse as more agents were added.
numbers: Accuracy MMLU / MMLU-Pro / ARC-C: full 78.5/65.2/96.0; vanilla prompt 72.6/52.5/89.0; scaffolding-only 68.1/49.4/84.0; exploration-only 71.5/52.1/89.7.
limits: Authors' own method; single paper.
agent_relevance: Same lesson as the human data: a fixed ACH routine can lose to a plain prompt. Use any hypothesis table as a loose scaffold.
quote: Rigid adherence to the structured protocol impairs generalization.

source: Yousuf et al. (2024) LLM Augmentations to support Analytical Reasoning over Multiple Documents
finding: Hypothesis-and-evidence tree memory for LLM intelligence analysis on three datasets (Crescent, Atlantic Storm, Manpad). LLMs, even augmented, stayed at surface summary and missed implicit links.
numbers: GPT-3.5 METEOR, basic prompt vs regular tree: Crescent .27 vs .29; Atlantic Storm .25 vs .34; Manpad .33 vs .27. ROUGE-1 Crescent .22 vs .18. No gain from raising temperature past 0.5-1.0.
limits: Not ACH proper; overlap metrics against reference narratives; mixed per dataset; old models.
agent_relevance: Hypothesis trees help on some sets and hurt on others. Structure alone does not supply missing inference.
quote: LLMs, as-is, are still inadequate to support intelligence analysts.

source: Evron (2026) Adversary Brains: hypothesis-based logical signatures for threat actor detection with LLMs
finding: A design paper that scales ACH from a few hypotheses to thousands, using LLMs to turn reports into testable hypotheses and judge matches. The text has no measured detection results.
numbers: No precision, recall or accuracy figures found in the full text.
limits: Design proposal only; no test.
agent_relevance: No evidence that LLM-run ACH works. Treat as an idea, not a result.
